name: Central Tagbanwa
confidence_why: Scebold 2003, the only description of Central Tagbanwa and a first-hand study from two years of fieldwork at Binga, reports that stress shifts between the penultimate and final syllable across repetitions of the same word, that he could find no rule governing it, and that any contrast is at most weak; no other work describes Central Tagbanwa stress at all.
catalog_citation: Scebold, Robert A. 2003. Central Tagbanwa: a Philippine language on the brink of extinction; sociolinguistics, grammar, and lexicon. (Linguistic Society of the Philippines Special Monograph Issue 48.) Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines. xii+168 pp. ISBN 971-780-014-6. Open PDF (SIL archive 43991), copy consulted via the Internet Archive snapshot 2023-05-20.
catalog_locator: Chapter 3 Phonology, §3.2 Stress, pp. 27-28; also §3.7.1 Other orthography notes, p. 39: 'Stress is not.'
catalog_quote: Stress has been difficult to analyze because of the variation encountered. Stress may vary between the first and second utterances of the same word spoken in succession, both in live and recorded data. ... A difference between live and recorded utterances of the same word is also common among the data. When there is a difference, stress is most commonly placed on the penultimate syllable in live utterances and on the ultimate in recorded utterances. However, the opposite also happens. (3) Live Utterance / Recorded Utterance: [dayámdam] [dayamdám] ‘bird’; [kúdlap] [kudláp] ‘lightning’; [mimíŋ] [mímiŋ] ‘kitten’. Free variation has also been observed between the first and second utterances on tape-recorded data: [p. 27] (4) [kalaláwɾan] ~ [kalalawɾán] ‘sea’; [tuɾíti] ~ [tuɾití] ‘carabao’; [dumalahá] ~ [dumaláha] ‘pullet’. I suspect that intonation patterns and other factors affect basic word stress a great deal. However, I have not been able to determine any phonological processes from the current data. If stress is contrastive, I believe it is only weakly so. Further analysis of stress is beyond the scope of this study. For the purpose of this monograph stress will not be written. [p. 28]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (180 pp., text present; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Tagbanwa Grammar.vp'; LSP Special Monograph 48, ISBN 971-780-014-6, copyright 2003 Linguistic Society of the Philippines) and re-extracted pp. 39-40 with extracted text, then viewed the two saved page scan printed p. 27) and printed p. 28). Every sentence of the reported quote is on those pages verbatim: p. 27 §3.2 Stress begins 'Stress has been difficult to analyze because of the variation encountered. Stress may vary between the first and second utterances of the same word spoken in succession, both in live and recorded data.' and continues 'When there is a difference, stress is most commonly placed on the penultimate syll…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. Stress falls on one of the last two syllables and varies between the penult and the ultima even across repetitions of the same word by the same speaker (examples: [dayámdam]~[dayamdám] 'bird', [kúdlap]~[kudláp] 'lightning', [kalaláwran]~[kalalawrán] 'sea', [turíti]~[turití] 'carabao'); the penult is the more common position in live (non-recorded) speech, the ultima in recorded speech. The author suspects intonation drives the variation, could not extract any phonological process, and judges stress at most weakly contrastive; the orthography does not write it.
new_statements.exceptions: The penult-in-live / ultima-in-recorded tendency has counterexamples ('the opposite also happens', e.g. [mimíŋ] live vs [mímiŋ] recorded 'kitten'); a drawn-out second utterance of [ludyák] 'mud' surfaces as [lú:dyak] with length and higher pitch on the first syllable. Spanish/English loans excluded from the syllable analysis (n. 1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms elicited live and from tape; the author attributes the variation to intonation/utterance factors. Data from Barangay Binga (Lumambong), San Vicente, Imuruan Bay, northern Palawan, 1991-1993.
new_statements.identity_note: Scebold 2003 describes the Central Tagbanwa of Barangay Binga (Lumambong sitio), San Vicente municipality, Imuruan Bay, northern Palawan (data also from Iraan to Pancol), 1991-1993; Glottolog's own language code for the work is 'Central Tagbanwa in Binga' = cent2090 [tgt]. Not to be confused with Aborlan Tagbanwa [tbw] tagb1258 or Calamian/Kalamian (Northern) Tagbanwa [tbk] cala1258, which are mutually unintelligible (Scebold p. ix); the Thiessen 1981 / Zorc accent remarks held in the tagb1258 folder concern those other varieties and Palawano, not cent2090.
